dialogue.scene: Lina and Yousef are preparing for their school debating club. The motion is: 'Fast fashion can never be sustainable.'

p1.t: Before we write a word, we need to define our terms. What exactly do we mean by 'sustainable'?
Anything that doesn't damage the planet, I suppose. By that standard, fast fashion fails completely.
That's a sweeping generalisation, though. Some brands now use recycled fabric.
True, but in the strict sense, a T-shirt worn three times isn't sustainable, whatever it's made of.

p2.t: So the crux of the matter isn't the material; it's how long clothes are actually worn.
Exactly. Our whole case hinges on that distinction.
Then we'll contend that the business model, not the fabric, is the real problem.
Perfect. If we define it that way, the other team can't hide behind recycled labels.

dialogue.focus: True, but in the strict sense, a T-shirt worn three times isn't sustainable, whatever it's made of.

dialogue.scene: Reem and Majed are writing a joint report for their environmental science class on farming in the desert, using two articles with opposite views.

p1.t: So the first article says desert farming is a total waste of water, right?
Not quite. That would misrepresent the author. She maintains that farming wheat in the desert wastes water.
And she puts forward greenhouse farming as the alternative?
Yes. And she concedes that modern greenhouses still use a lot of energy for cooling.

p2.t: The second writer just dismisses greenhouses as too expensive.
Careful. He dismisses them as too expensive for small farmers, which is a narrower claim.
Fine. Does either of them actually refute the other?
No. They focus on different crops, so neither refutes the other directly.

dialogue.scene: Hessa and Daniel, an exchange student from Canada, are editing a paragraph for an academic essay on solar energy in Saudi Arabia.

p1.t: My first sentence says, 'People in Saudi Arabia use more solar power now.' It sounds a bit plain.
Try nominalising it: 'There has been a marked shift towards solar power in Saudi Arabia.'
Better. Next: 'Solar panels got cheaper, so more companies adopted them.'
How about: 'A sharp reduction in panel costs has led to the wider adoption of solar technology.'

p2.t: That packs a lot into one line. Doesn't it hide who did what, though?
It can, so we add a source. Also mention the growing reliance on gas for electricity.
Right: 'Large solar plants such as Sudair could bring about a reduction in that reliance.'
Good, and say why it's now viable: sunshine all year and falling costs.

dialogue.scene: Sultan and Emma are reviewing a school blog post titled 'Breakfast Makes You Smarter' for their critical thinking class.

p1.t: The post says students who eat breakfast get higher grades, so breakfast makes you smarter.
It doesn't necessarily follow. Higher grades and breakfast might both come from something else, like regular sleep.
So the survey shows a pattern, not a causal relationship?
Exactly. And the writer conflates 'getting higher grades' with 'being smarter', which isn't the same thing.

p2.t: She also quotes only two studies. I found five more with mixed results.
Then she's cherry-picking. That's a serious weakness.
So what conclusion can we fairly draw?
That breakfast may help, but any link to intelligence is tenuous at best.

dialogue.focus: It doesn't necessarily follow. Higher grades and breakfast might both come from something else, like regular sleep.

dialogue.scene: Abdullah and Nina are presenting the results of an imaginary trial of a four-day school week to their student council.

p1.t: So, did the four-day week work? Can we say it was a success?
By and large, yes. Students reported feeling less tired, with the possible exception of the youngest classes.
And grades? Some people are saying they shot up.
It would be an overstatement to say they shot up. They improved only marginally.

p2.t: So the benefit was mainly about wellbeing, not results?
To a large extent, yes. Longer days were hard for some students to concentrate through.
Then should we recommend it to the school?
Only under certain conditions: shorter lessons, a proper lunch break and more time outdoors.

dialogue.scene: In a school debate, Noura proposes and Kareem opposes the motion: 'University places should depend on interviews as well as exam scores.'

p1.t: The motion before us is that universities should interview applicants, not rely on exam scores alone.
Exam scores fall short of showing motivation, communication or curiosity, all of which predict success at university.
My opponent contends that interviews reveal motivation. In practice, they often reward confidence and coaching.
The weight of evidence suggests that exam results remain the fairest single predictor.

p2.t: I concede that interviews can be coached. That's why I'm proposing structured interviews with fixed questions.
Even structured interviews take time and money that many universities simply don't have.
A cost, certainly, but not a reason to ignore everything an exam can't measure.
On balance, combining both gives a fairer, more complete picture of every applicant.

p1.t: Were AI to write all the news, would we still need journalists?

dialogue.scene: Haya and Ziad are presenting the results of their school survey on teenagers' reading habits to their class.

p1.t: Turning now to our results, as illustrated by this chart, reading for pleasure fell sharply between the ages of twelve and sixteen.
To put this into perspective, nearly every twelve-year-old in our survey read for fun weekly; among sixteen-year-olds, fewer than half did.
However, we saw a marked increase in audiobook listening over the same period.
In fact, audiobooks account for nearly a third of the reading older students reported.

p2.t: Bear in mind that our sample was small: just 120 students from one school.
So the figures suggest a trend rather than prove one.
Having looked at the numbers, let's move on to what students told us in interviews.
Their answers help explain why the drop happens.

dialogue.focus: Turning now to our results, as illustrated by this chart, reading for pleasure fell sharply between the ages of twelve and sixteen.
qs: What increased while reading for pleasure fell?

dialogue.scene: Lama has just presented her project on Red Sea coral reefs. Ahmed, a student in the audience, asks her some questions.

p1.t: You said Red Sea corals cope well with heat. Does that mean they're safe from climate change?
That's a pertinent question. If I understand you correctly, you're asking whether they're fully protected.
Yes, exactly.
To address your point, they're more heat-tolerant than many reefs, but not immune. Pollution and coastal building still threaten them.

p2.t: And what about fishing? Is that a problem too?
With respect to fishing, I'm afraid that falls outside the scope of our study, which focused on temperature.
Could you say more about why they tolerate heat so well?
I'd be happy to elaborate. One theory is that their ancestors passed through very warm southern waters thousands of years ago.

dialogue.focus: To address your point, they're more heat-tolerant than many reefs, but not immune. Pollution and coastal building still threaten them.
qs: What threats to the corals does Lama mention?
Why doesn't Lama answer the question about fishing?

dialogue.scene: Omar is presenting a project on microplastics found on beaches near Jeddah. His teacher, Ms Laura, asks him some challenging questions.

p1.t: Your samples came from only three beaches. Isn't it misleading to talk about the whole coastline?
That's a fair criticism. We should have been clearer that these are early findings.
So do you withdraw your claim?
No. I stand by the finding itself: all three beaches contained microplastics. The data just don't allow us to generalise further.

p2.t: Are these plastics harmful to people who eat local fish?
I take your point; it's an important question. But I'm not in a position to answer it, because we didn't test fish.
Then what would you recommend?
Let me come back to that in my conclusion, where I suggest a wider study.

dialogue.focus: No. I stand by the finding itself: all three beaches contained microplastics. The data just don't allow us to generalise further.
qs: Which part of his claim does Omar stand by?
Why can't Omar answer the question about fish?

dialogue.scene: Khalid and Sara are rehearsing the conclusion of their science project on turning date palm waste into building boards.

p1.t: So, to draw the threads together: palm waste, which is often burned, could become useful building material.
The take-home message is simple: what we throw away might be a resource.
And that has far-reaching implications for farmers, builders and the environment.
One question merits further research, though: how well do the boards cope with humidity?

p2.t: How should we finish?
Let's come full circle. We opened with a photo of palm fronds being burned on a farm.
Then I'll leave you with the same farm, now with a storeroom built from palm-fibre boards.
Perfect. It shows our whole argument in a single image.

dialogue.focus: So, to draw the threads together: palm waste, which is often burned, could become useful building material.
qs: What is the take-home message of the project?
How do Khalid and Sara plan to come full circle?

dialogue.scene: At a youth science conference, the chair, Mr Hassan, introduces Nouf, who presents her project on shade in school playgrounds. Liam asks a question.

p1.t: Our next speaker is Nouf, who will present her project on shade in school playgrounds.
Thank you. I'd like to begin by asking why so many playgrounds are empty at midday.
Having established that shaded surfaces were consistently cooler, this brings me to our main question: did students actually use them more?
In light of our observations, the answer is clearly yes, especially in the hottest months.

p2.t: Thank you, Nouf. We have time for one question. Yes, Liam?
Did you consider artificial grass? Many schools use it.
That's a pertinent question. Artificial grass falls outside the scope of this project, but it can get very hot, so it would be worth testing.
Thank you. Let's give Nouf a round of applause.

dialogue.focus: Having established that shaded surfaces were consistently cooler, this brings me to our main question: did students actually use them more?
qs: What did Nouf's project find about shaded surfaces?
How does Nouf handle Liam's question about artificial grass?

words.ex: Before we argue about 'fair' grades, we should define our terms.
The result of the debate hinges on one key definition.
'All teenagers waste money' is a sweeping generalisation.
Some economists contend that cheap clothes hide real costs.
The crux of the matter is how often we replace things.
In the strict sense, a hybrid car is not a zero-emission car.

dialogue.t: We need to define our terms. What do we mean by 'sustainable'?
Anything that doesn't harm the planet. Fast fashion fails that test.
That's a sweeping generalisation. Some brands use recycled fabric.
In the strict sense, a T-shirt worn three times isn't sustainable.
So the crux of the matter is how long clothes are worn.
Exactly. Our case hinges on that distinction.

grammar.title: Narrowing a claim precisely
grammar.ar: في النقاش الأكاديمي حدّد معنى الكلمة الأساسية أولاً، ثم ضيّق ادعاءك بعبارات مثل in the strict sense بدلاً من التعميم.
examples: In the strict sense, recycling is not the same as reducing.
The argument hinges on how we define 'waste'.
Critics contend that low prices hide high environmental costs.

words.ex: The author concedes that the study was small.
He dismissed the plan as unrealistic.
The second study refuted the idea completely.
He still maintains that the method works.
She put forward a convincing theory.
Please don't misrepresent what I said.

dialogue.t: The first article says desert farming wastes water, right?
Not quite. She maintains that farming wheat in the desert wastes water.
And she concedes something?
Yes, she concedes that greenhouses use a lot of energy.
The second writer dismisses greenhouses as too expensive.
Only for small farmers. Neither writer refutes the other.

grammar.title: Precise reporting verbs
grammar.ar: اختر فعل النقل بدقة: concede = يعترف بشيء ضد رأيه، maintain = يتمسك، dismiss = يستخفّ، refute = يثبت خطأه بالدليل.
examples: The author concedes that her sample was small.
He dismisses the idea as impractical.
The new results refute the earlier claim.

words.ex: There has been a clear shift towards electric buses.
The adoption of smart meters cut waste.
Cities show a growing reliance on air conditioning.
New laws brought about real change.
We saw a sharp reduction in costs.
Is rooftop solar viable in hot, dusty cities?

dialogue.t: 'People use more solar power now.' It sounds plain.
Say: 'There has been a marked shift towards solar power.'
And 'Panels got cheaper, so companies adopted them'?
'A reduction in costs has led to the wider adoption of solar.'
Could solar plants bring about a reduction in gas use?
Yes, and with sunshine all year, it's viable.

grammar.title: Nominalisation
grammar.ar: في الكتابة الأكاديمية نحوّل الفعل إلى اسم: reduce ← a reduction in، adopt ← the adoption of، rely on ← a reliance on. هذا يجعل الجملة أدقّ وأكثر رسمية.
examples: Costs fell sharply. → There was a sharp reduction in costs.
Companies adopted solar. → The adoption of solar by companies increased.
We rely on gas. → Our reliance on gas remains high.

words.ex: He studies late, but it doesn't necessarily follow that he's tired.
People often conflate being busy with being productive.
The link between the two events is tenuous.
Don't cherry-pick the results you like.
A survey alone can't show a causal relationship.
It's too early to draw a firm conclusion.

dialogue.t: The post says breakfast makes you smarter.
It doesn't necessarily follow. Sleep could explain both.
So it's a pattern, not a causal relationship?
Yes, and she conflates higher grades with being smarter.
She also quotes only two studies.
Then she's cherry-picking. The link is tenuous at best.

grammar.title: Challenging reasoning precisely
grammar.ar: لا تقل فقط 'أنت مخطئ'؛ حدّد مكان الخلل: it doesn't follow (الاستنتاج)، conflate (خلط مفهومين)، cherry-pick (انتقاء الأدلة).
examples: It doesn't necessarily follow that more homework means more learning.
You're conflating correlation with causation.
The article cherry-picks the most dramatic figures.

words.ex: To a large extent, success depends on habits.
Everyone agreed, with the possible exception of Ali.

words.w: it would be an overstatement to say
words.ex: It would be an overstatement to say the trial failed.
By and large, the feedback was positive.
Attendance rose marginally.
The plan works only under certain conditions.

dialogue.t: Was the four-day week a success?
By and large, yes, with the possible exception of the youngest classes.
Some say grades shot up.
That would be an overstatement. They rose marginally.
Should we recommend it?
Only under certain conditions, like shorter lessons.

grammar.title: Qualifying claims
grammar.ar: الحجة الدقيقة لا تبالغ: حدّد الدرجة (to a large extent, marginally) والاستثناء (with the possible exception of) والشرط (under certain conditions).
examples: To a large extent, the trial was successful.
It would be an overstatement to say grades soared.
The plan works only under certain conditions.

words.ex: The motion was narrowly defeated.
My opponent contends that exams are fair, but they measure only one skill.
The weight of evidence points the other way.
The plan falls short of its own goals.
I concede that interviews take time.
On balance, the benefits outweigh the costs.

dialogue.t: The motion is that universities should interview applicants.
Exam scores fall short of showing motivation.
My opponent contends that interviews reveal motivation, but they reward coaching.
I concede that. So I propose structured interviews.
They cost time and money.
On balance, combining both is fairer.

grammar.title: Structuring a precise debate speech
grammar.ar: في المناظرة: اذكر الموضوع (the motion)، انقل رأي الخصم بدقة (My opponent contends that)، اعترف بنقطة (I concede)، ثم احسم (On balance).
examples: The motion before us is that exams should be abolished.
My opponent contends that interviews are unfair, but the evidence is mixed.
On balance, a combined approach is the most reliable.

words.w: by the middle of the century
words.ex: By the middle of the century, many cities will have doubled in size.
In all likelihood, more people will work from home.
The project is on course to finish early.
The new road had unforeseen consequences for local shops.
Online shopping has reshaped city centres.
Demand for housing may outpace supply.

dialogue.t: By 2050, Riyadh will, in all likelihood, have grown much bigger.
Is it on course to keep growing that fast?
Probably. The metro will have reshaped how people travel.
But growth can bring unforeseen consequences.
True. Demand for homes may outpace construction.
So planners will have had to rethink everything.

grammar.title: The future perfect
grammar.ar: نستخدم will have + التصريف الثالث للحديث عن شيء سيكون قد اكتمل قبل وقت محدّد في المستقبل، وغالباً مع by 2050 أو by the time.
examples: By 2050, the city will have doubled in size.
By then, most cars will have become electric.
Will they have finished the new line by 2030?

words.ex: Were AI to replace teachers, schools would change completely.
Few of the predictions came to pass.
Smartphones rendered paper maps almost obsolete.
A short news alert is a far cry from a real investigation.
Online shops have displaced many small stores.
Patients value the human touch of a kind nurse.

dialogue.t: Were AI to write all the news, would we need journalists?
Were that to come to pass, reporters would still find the stories.
Couldn't AI render reporters obsolete?
A match report is a far cry from an investigation.
So AI won't displace journalists?
Some, maybe, but readers value the human touch.

grammar.title: Inverted conditionals: Were … to …
grammar.ar: Were + الفاعل + to + الفعل صيغة رسمية لـ If … were to …، وتُستخدم لتخيّل حدث مستقبلي غير مرجّح.
examples: Were AI to replace teachers, schools would change.
Were the price to fall, more people would buy one.
Were that to happen, we would need new laws.

words.ex: Should the mission fail, the crew would return to Earth.
For the team, this project is uncharted territory.
Early flights paved the way for modern travel.
In the event of a fire, use the stairs.
The design pushes the boundaries of engineering.
Clean energy would be a giant leap for the planet.

dialogue.t: Should humans settle on Mars, what would they need?
Shelter. Should a dust storm hit, they'd need it fast.
It's uncharted territory for the human body.
Moon missions will pave the way.
In the event of an emergency, help would be months away.
Still, it would be a giant leap for science.

grammar.title: Inverted conditionals: Should …
grammar.ar: Should + الفاعل + الفعل المجرد صيغة رسمية لـ If، وتعني أن الحدث ممكن لكنه غير مؤكد. مثل: Should you need help, call me.
examples: Should the engine fail, the crew will use the backup.
Should you need more information, please ask.
Should the storm continue, the launch would be delayed.

words.ex: Some old wells have already run dry.
Good planning can stave off shortages.
Demand for water may outstrip supply.
Every city needs a contingency plan for drought.
Scientists fear we are near a tipping point.
In the long run, saving water costs less.

dialogue.t: Should demand keep rising, could our water run dry?
Some underground supplies could. They refill slowly.
So desalination staves off a crisis?
For now. But should energy costs rise, it would be expensive.
We need a contingency plan.
In the long run, saving water is cheaper.

grammar.title: Comparing Should … and Were … to …
grammar.ar: Should تُستخدم لاحتمال ممكن، و Were … to لاحتمال أبعد أو افتراضي. كلاهما رسمي ويأتي في بداية الجملة.
examples: Should prices rise, people will use less water.
Were the rain to stop completely, farms would close.
Should you see a leak, report it immediately.

words.ex: By the time we graduate, the software will have changed.
The school wants to future-proof its classrooms.
Technology skills are a moving target.
Many employees upskill through online courses.
Lifelong learning keeps your mind active.
She reads research papers to stay ahead of the curve.

dialogue.t: By thirty, we'll have been working for ten years.
Maybe in jobs that don't exist yet.
How do you future-proof a career?
Lifelong learning. I'll have been upskilling for years.
So staying ahead of the curve means learning how to learn.
Exactly.

grammar.title: The future perfect continuous
grammar.ar: will have been + فعل ing تعبّر عن مدة نشاط مستمر حتى نقطة في المستقبل، مثل: By 2040, I'll have been working for ten years.
examples: By June, I'll have been studying English for twelve years.
By the time she retires, she'll have been teaching for thirty years.
How long will you have been living here by next year?

words.ex: In the best-case scenario, the project finishes early.
We need to prepare for the worst-case scenario.
It's conceivable that exams will disappear.
Good leaders plan for every eventuality.
In all likelihood, teachers will still be needed.
Were that to happen, buildings would become community centres.

dialogue.t: Will schools still exist in 2050?
In all likelihood, yes, though they will have changed.
Were lessons to move online, buildings would become community centres.
What's the best-case scenario?
A personal AI tutor for every student.
The worst case is isolated students.
So we should plan for every eventuality.

grammar.title: Mixing future forms for speculation
grammar.ar: في النقاش عن المستقبل نمزج: will have + pp للإنجاز، Were … to للاحتمال البعيد، Should للاحتمال الممكن، و in all likelihood لدرجة الاحتمال.
examples: By 2050, schools will have changed a great deal.
Were all lessons to move online, students might feel isolated.
Should funding fall, the worst-case scenario would be larger classes.

words.ex: After years of moving, they finally put down roots in Jeddah.
A love of poetry runs in the family.
Team sports give many students a sense of belonging.
It's a tight-knit neighbourhood where everyone helps.
She carries the torch for her grandmother's recipes.

words.w: the apple doesn't fall far from the tree
words.ex: He loves football like his dad; the apple doesn't fall far from the tree.

dialogue.t: I've never really put down roots anywhere.
My family has lived in Al-Qassim for generations.
Does that give you a sense of belonging?
Yes. We're a tight-knit family, and poetry runs in the family.
The apple doesn't fall far from the tree!
Roots aren't a trap; they keep you steady.

grammar.title: Idioms and metaphors of roots
grammar.ar: نتكلم عن الهوية بلغة مجازية: الجذور (roots) للأصل والانتماء، والشجرة والأغصان للعائلة. استخدم التعبير الاصطلاحي كما هو دون تغيير كلماته.
examples: They put down roots in Riyadh twenty years ago.
Kindness runs in the family.
My grandparents are the roots; we are the branches.

words.ex: After years of practice, typing is second nature to her.
Some jokes simply get lost in translation.
Old songs are a window into the past.
Many bilingual teens switch between languages easily.
The beautiful view left us at a loss for words.
Music is the heart and soul of the festival.

dialogue.t: You switch between Arabic and English all the time.
It's become second nature.
Does anything get lost in translation?
Yes, especially expressions of hospitality.
For me, Spanish is a window into my grandparents' world.
Language is the heart and soul of a culture.

grammar.title: Metaphors for language
grammar.ar: الاستعارة (metaphor) تقول إن شيئاً هو شيء آخر لتوضيح فكرة: Language is a window / a bridge / the heart and soul. لا نستخدم like هنا، بعكس التشبيه.
examples: Language is a bridge between generations.
Her poems are a window into village life.
Some proverbs get lost in translation.

words.ex: Black coffee is an acquired taste for many people.
Her talk gave us plenty of food for thought.
Poor planning is a recipe for disaster.
She brings years of experience to the table.
Restoring the old house was a labour of love.

words.w: variety is the spice of life
words.ex: Try a new dish; variety is the spice of life.

dialogue.t: Is Saudi coffee always flavoured with cardamom?
Usually. For some visitors, it's an acquired taste.
And it's always served with dates?
Yes. It's how we say 'welcome' without words.
So food is a language of its own. That's food for thought.
